newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-ABS to detail Australia telephone jobs effect.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-ABS to detail Australia telephone jobs effect.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Statistics will further detail the effect of a methodological change on its labour force data in the February estimates to be issued on Thursday, a bureau spokeswoman said.
She declined, however, to say exactly what further information the bureau would provide.

The bureau has said its phase-in of telephone interviewing is affecting its labour force data, making the jobs market look weaker by pushing down employment estimates by a cumulative 6,000 to 9,000 each month since the changeover began in August.
With the February data the labour force survey will finally reach its new configuation of one panel of respondents interviewed face-to-face and the remaining seven by telephone.

Since the bureau publicly acknowleged the telephone interviewing effect in mid January, economists have hoped for a more refined estimate of the effect on employment numbers -- presumably, between the 6,000 and 9,000 per month cumulative.
The issue is not the accuracy of estimates of employment levels and the like, since no-one knows whether the new system or the old is more accurate.
But the change-over is distorting the rates of change that policymakers use to gauge the strength of the economy.
Economists also want to know how the method has affected estimates of unemployment numbers and the number of people not in the workforce.
The effect has to show up in these numbers because the total of people employed, unemployed and not in the labour force equals the population, which is practically constant.
So the downward effect on employment numbers from the new method must be offset by a net upward effect on unemployment numbers and people not in the labour force.
The bureau has publicly said the effect on unemployment and not-in-the-labour-force estimates has been unclear.
Privately, officials say the upward effect on the not-in-the-labour-force number has been larger than the upward effect on unemployment.

The trend unemployment rate in January was 8.6 percent but if the data were adjusted for the telephone effect it would probably be only 8.4 percent, and falling faster than shown in the bureau's publication.
